paras: The lynching of Jack Nelson was the hanging and shooting of a Black man by a gathering of neighbors near Cairo, Georgia, on the night of July 30, 1910. He was accused of entering the bedroom of the young daughter of a farmer, John Wade, and was dragged from under her bed, hanged from a tree limb and shot. The story ran across the country on the wires, often under a mistaken Cairo, Illinois, dateline, and reached two Black weeklies only as a single sentence in a syndicated news column.

Wade lived ten miles northeast of Cairo, and a United Press dispatch described him as "a white farmer." Only the Alaska Citizen named the accused man, calling him Jack Nelson; every other report called him "a negro."

According to the Georgia dispatch, the man entered the room through a window and woke the girl, whose screams brought her family into the room. With no time to escape, he dived under the bed and was dragged out from his hiding place. News of the capture was carried from house to house, and "a body of men quickly gathered and decided to lynch the negro immediately"; the Atlanta Semi-Weekly Journal added that "a conference was held" first.

The men put him in a wagon, tied one end of a rope around his neck and the other to a limb, and drove the wagon from under him. His body was then "riddled with bullets," or in the Atlanta version, "a volley of shots rang out."

The Georgia dispatch said that, because there were eyewitnesses, the coroner's jury did not investigate the death. The United Press version instead said the authorities were conducting an investigation, but no report of its results, of arrests or of any grand jury action appears in the coverage.

The Richmond Times-Dispatch ran the earliest text, dated July 31, under the headline "Meets Fate Quickly at Hands of Lynchers," and the Washington Evening Star printed it as "Lynching in Quick Order." The Orangeburg Times and Democrat headed it "Took the Rope Route" over the deck "Black Fiend Found, in Young Girl's Room," and the Salt Lake Herald-Republican used "Negro Fiend Caught Under Victim's Bed." Smaller papers in the Carolinas, the Dakotas and elsewhere carried brief versions through August 5.

A United Press dispatch placed the lynching at Cairo, Illinois, said it recalled "the murder of Anna Pelly at Cairo and the lynching of Will James," and added that "Race feeling has been aroused." Western papers that used this or the Illinois-datelined version headlined it "Would-Be Rapist Lynched" and "Nelson in Hades," and the East Oregonian grouped it with the Palestine, Texas, killings under "A Fatal Day for Negroes." The Hopkinsville Kentuckian counted a Georgia lynching in the opening of "the lynching season," saying the victims were "executed for attacks on white women and girls."

In the Black press, the Twin City Star on August 4 and the Cleveland Gazette on August 6 printed one sentence saying a man "caught as he approached the young daughter of John Wade" was hanged and shot "by a mob." The same sentence appeared in a white Ohio weekly's general news column, and neither Black paper added a headline, comment or correspondent's account.

Most reports, including a Georgia paper and the earliest dispatch, placed the lynching near Cairo, Georgia, while the United Press and several reprints said Cairo, Illinois. The Evening Star and Yorkville Enquirer said it happened Saturday night, while the Orangeburg Times and Democrat said Sunday night. The Georgia wire had the man waking the sleeping girl, but the United Press and Alaska Citizen said the girl entered her room and found him there.

reader.title: Lynching of Jack Nelson
bases: Every account says a gathered body of men or crowd hanged a Black man seized in a farmhouse and shot his body, with no officers or legal process reported (A1, A3, A6).

Neighbors gathered into 'a body of men' that decided to lynch the man at once, hanged him from a limb and riddled his body with bullets (A1, A3, A14). He was killed for being found in a white girl's bedroom, with no arrest, trial or officer involved (A3, A6).

Two distinct wire texts, the Georgia-datelined dispatch (A3, A1, A14) and a United Press dispatch (A6), agree on the core event, though no local or follow-up report was found and the UP version misplaces it in Illinois.

accounts.label: Georgia wire (Cairo, Ga. dateline)
accounts.gist: The man entered through a window and woke the girl; the family found him under the bed, neighbors gathered and decided to lynch him at once, hanged him from a wagon and shot the body; the coroner's jury did not investigate because there were eyewitnesses.

accounts.label: United Press (Cairo, Ill. dateline)
accounts.gist: The girl entered her room, heard the man and screamed; he was dragged out of the house and a crowd strung him up to a tree; authorities were investigating, and the case was linked to the Anna Pelly murder and Will James lynching at Cairo, Ill.

accounts.label: Syndicated news column
accounts.gist: A one-sentence summary: a negro caught as he approached John Wade's daughter in Cairo, Ga., was hanged and shot by a mob.

framing.detail: Southern and western headlines called the man a 'Fiend' and 'Would-Be Rapist' and treated the speed of the hanging approvingly ('Meets Fate Quickly', 'Took the Rope Route', 'Nelson in Hades').
Most papers printed the Georgia or United Press wire text without comment, several grouping it with the Palestine, Texas, killings as 'A Fatal Day for Negroes'.

The Hopkinsville Kentuckian counted it in a 'lynching season' of men 'executed for attacks on white women and girls' while calling the Palestine killings slaughter of men slain because 'their skins were black'.
The Twin City Star and Cleveland Gazette printed only the syndicated one-sentence item, with no headline or comment.

conflicts.note: The Georgia-datelined texts include a Georgia paper (A14) and the earliest dispatch (A3); the Illinois datelines carry the same Wade details and appear to be a misattribution, the UP text tying it to an earlier Cairo, Ill., case.
The earliest dispatch, dated July 31, says 'last night' and the Evening Star says 'Saturday night'; the Sunday versions repeat the same wire text with a later dateline or wording.
